newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Australian gold sale a change of philosophy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australian gold sale a change of philosophy.

text.p: There was barely a dollar movement in the gold price after the Reserve Bank of Australia announced on Thursday it had sold 167 tonnes of the metal on to the the market from its reserves.
But the significance of the sale by the central bank of the world's third largest gold producer was considerable, dealers and analysts said.
The gold market closed at $331.55 per ounce in Europe, just 80 cents off its Wednesday close and only 10 cents above the the 4-1/4 year low fixing plumbed on Wednesday morning.
"This clearly reflects the change in thinking that has come to central banks in asset management," one analyst at a leading European bank said.
In the announcement of the gold sale the Reserve Bank said the sale followed a review of the constant benefits of holding a significant part of international reserves in gold.

"The Bank's board concluded that while there was a case to hold some gold as a contingency against unforeseen events the previous holdings (20 percent of international reserves) were no longer justified," the Bank's announcement said.
He noted reappraising gold assets was not just the prerogative of the European central banks and their governments which were juggling for entry into European Monetary Union.
Central banks in gold producing countries like Canada, Brazil and now Australia were part of a widening circle of banks which were reflecting a change in philosophy.
"The Australians are very shrewd and have got some selling done. Now they are following on Canada's path," said Ted Arnold metals market analyst at Merrill Lynch.
Canada is the world's fourth largest gold producer and its central bank through a programme of small monthly disposals has sold 592 tonnes since 1979.
Another analyst reasoned that the Australian move reflected the market's view that the gold price was heading lower.

"If you felt holding gold was no longer justified but you would get a better price for it later, you would hold on. That they have not done that suggests they think they cannot get a better price later," he said.
The reserve bank said it realised over $1.8 billion from the gold sale and reduced its gold holding to 80 tonnes from 247 tonnes.
A senior London-based gold dealer said the sale would make the aggressive forward selling policy of the high cost Australian gold miners more difficult to complete.
Mines borrow gold to sell from central banks or, less usually, commercial banks to sell before they have mined the equivalent amount so they can protect themselves against falling prices.
They repay the bank later with gold they have mined.

Forward selling by the miners coupled with the threat of central bank sales are the two key factors which have encircled the gold market in gloom this year and driven investors to more potentially profitable assets like equities and bonds.
"The miners are probably very unhappy," the senior dealer said.
"Not only has the reserve bank helped push the price down but it will now have less gold to lend which will put pressure on the miners to borrow elsewhere," he said.

According to Union Bank of Switzerland precious metals analyst Andy Smith, the cost to the world's top dozen central bank gold holders of retaining gold as a reserve asset, compared to holding interest bearing instruments, is $15 billion annually.
"The amounts involved mean sentimental criteria no longer apply. The interest foregone is too large to ignore," an analyst said.
He added that most of the central banks' gold reserves were valued at well below current market prices making vast on-paper proits available even in the current weak market.
"There are great profits to be gained by taking the jump (and selling gold)," he said.
The major gold disposals since 1989, until news on Thursday of an Australian sale, have involved either the Belgian or Dutch central banks.
The Dutch most recently announced the sale of 300 tonnes of gold in January this year. Their previous sale was in 1992-1993 when they and the Belgian National Bank together sold 602 tonnes.
Belgium subsequently sold 175 tonnes in 1995 and 203 tonnes during the first quarter of 1996. It made its first major gold sale in 1989 when it disposed of 127 tonnes.
Last year research organisation Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) calculated there was a net sale of 239 tonnes of bullion from reserves by official sector holders.
The net figure comprised 588 tonnes of gross disposals and 349 tonnes of gross purchases.
The average for the past 10 years is a net disposal of 213 tonnes, according to GFMS.
In 1996 16 countries were net sellers of gold but only five sold more than 10 tonnes.
Central banks bought gold for their reserves in 1996 with Russia and China the most prominent buyers, GMFS said.
